summary:
North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1996 as a Council of Europe accession condition, and the anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code, which explicitly listed both grounds under the hate speech provisions. The Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 also introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

Legal gender recognition remains unresolved. The government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the legal gender recognition chapter one day before Parliamentary Committee review, and ILGA-Europe and the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia identify LGR as the top priority. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights and awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Same-sex relationships remain unrecognized: family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman," and in July 2014 the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption. A 2015 constitutional amendment barring legal recognition of same-sex relations passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely." The first Pride Parade took place in June 2019; a 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organisers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding. Global Voices also notes a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with sexual-orientation and gender-identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code, one of the few documented enforcement actions. The 2019 US State Department Human Rights Report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases.

Violence and discrimination against LGBTI people are documented. The 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. The report states there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations. The 2019 report also found the LGBTQ community is "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities," with hate speech on social media following the first Pride Parade.

Local officials have acted against LGBTI groups. In June 2023 Strumica Mayor Kostadin Kostadinov nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organisations and vowed to veto future ones. Polling by the Center for Civil and Human Rights in 2002 found over 80% of respondents viewed homosexuality as "a psychiatric disorder that endangered families" and about 65% considered it a crime warranting jail. North Macedonia ranked 10th worst European country for LGBTQ tourists in 2019.

Support services exist in the capital. The LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid, and EGAL is described as the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale in February 2012, the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination. The ranking has since improved alongside the 2019 legal reforms, but the historical position frames how regional observers read the country.

Washington Blade reported on 13 October 2023 that Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantify how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of both countries, casting discrimination as a measurable drag on growth and jobs. This economic framing is an advocacy argument rather than a statement of visitor risk.

outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that North Macedonia ranked 10th worst European country for LGBTQ tourists in 2019 comes from a Wikipedia summary of the 2019 US Country Report and is not independently verified against a primary ranking methodology in this inventory.

The 2002 polling figures (over 80% viewing homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder, about 65% considering it a crime) are more than two decades old and are not corroborated by any newer survey in the inventory; their current representativeness is unresolved.

The Washington Blade economic-impact figures for North Macedonia are not reproduced in this inventory, so the specific magnitude of the claimed drag on growth and jobs is not sourced here.

Whether the withdrawn Draft Law on Civil Registry has been reintroduced or replaced since the 2024 Enlargement Review is not addressed by any source in the inventory.
